capabilities.action: Relate zero net force to unchanged velocity.
capabilities.success_criterion: Accept steady motion as compatible with zero net force.

capabilities.action: Distinguish zero net force from the absence of individual forces.
capabilities.success_criterion: Recognize that nonzero forces can cancel in the net force.

capabilities.action: Assign each force arrow to the body on which that force acts.
capabilities.success_criterion: Place a partner force on the other body's diagram rather than the chosen body's diagram.

capabilities.action: Decide whether an observer description requires a pseudo-force.
capabilities.success_criterion: Identify accelerating-observer cases that need the added pseudo-force convention.

capabilities.action: Relate signed net external force to acceleration with F_net = m a.
capabilities.success_criterion: Builds the force sum for one chosen body before solving for signed acceleration or net force.

extensions.agent_a:semantic_boundary: Owns qualitative contact-level friction existence and direction from relative sliding or slip tendency. It does not own coefficient-based magnitude/state selection; that belongs to CAP-NLM-FRICTION-QUANT.

capabilities.action: Identify friction as a contact force that opposes relative sliding or the tendency to slide.
capabilities.success_criterion: Draws friction along the contact surface in the direction that opposes relative sliding/tendency, not automatically opposite the object's velocity.

capabilities.action: Identify Newton-third-law force pairs as equal and opposite forces of the same interaction acting on different bodies.
capabilities.success_criterion: Names both bodies and keeps the two partner forces on separate free-body diagrams.

extensions.agent_a:semantic_boundary: Owns static-feasibility and kinetic-friction model selection after the body/contact model is declared: determine N, solve the no-slip friction demand, compare with the static bound, and switch models only when the contact state justifies it. It does not create separate capabilities for every incline, block-stack, or force-angle context.

capabilities.action: Decide whether static friction can supply the tangential force required by the chosen-body dynamics; if relative sliding is established, use the declared kinetic-friction model.
capabilities.success_criterion: Obtains the actual normal force from the free-body dynamics, computes the friction required for no slip, accepts static friction only when |f_required| <= mu_s N, uses equality only at impending slip, and switches to |f_k| = mu_k N only after relative sliding is established.

extensions.agent_a:semantic_boundary: Owns the kinematic consequence of an active fixed-separation constraint and the body-versus-system boundary used with Newton II. It does not license common acceleration after the constraint is lost, and it does not own equal-string-tension or pulley-length geometry.

capabilities.action: Identify which bodies are constrained to share one acceleration component and write consistent body-specific or whole-system Newton-II equations.
capabilities.success_criterion: States the physical constraint that fixes relative separation, uses one compatible sign convention, gives constrained bodies the same acceleration component only when justified, and cancels internal partner forces only in a whole-system force sum rather than on an individual-body FBD.

extensions.agent_a:semantic_boundary: Owns force transmission in one declared ideal string/redirection model: body-specific tension forces, one common tension magnitude when justified, and tension obtained from Newton II rather than identified automatically with weight. It does not own the string-length kinematic constraint.

capabilities.action: Use one declared ideal-string model to assign tension forces and, where justified, one common tension magnitude throughout that same string.
capabilities.success_criterion: States the ideal massless-taut-string and frictionless/massless redirection assumptions, puts each tension arrow on the body it acts on, uses one tension magnitude only under those assumptions, and refuses that equality for a nonideal rope or pulley model.

extensions.agent_a:semantic_boundary: Owns conversion of one fixed-pulley inextensible-string geometry into signed displacement, velocity and acceleration constraints. The length relation is a kinematic claim and does not by itself prove equal tension.

capabilities.action: Convert constant length of one taut inextensible string over one fixed ideal pulley into the corresponding displacement, velocity, or acceleration relation.
capabilities.success_criterion: Declares coordinates along the two string segments, writes the fixed-length relation y_A + y_B = constant, derives a_A + a_B = 0 in those coordinates, and does not generalize that result to movable/compound pulley geometry.

microtopics.title: Zero net force allows steady motion
microtopics.badge_reason: Everyday friction makes continued motion look as if it needs a continuing push.
entry_assumptions: Can tell whether an object's velocity is changing.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Zero net force does not mean zero motion; it means velocity does not change, so rest and steady motion are both compatible with the same condition.

teaching_path.action: Separate the statement 'is moving' from the statement 'is changing its velocity.'
teaching_path.why_valid: Motion and change of motion are different observations, and only the second identifies acceleration.
teaching_path.output: state A: moving steadily.  state B: speeding up, slowing down, or turning.

teaching_path.action: Imagine a low-friction cart after the hand has stopped touching it and compare successive equal-time snapshots.
teaching_path.why_valid: Once the hand is gone, a continuing steady velocity can be observed without a continuing forward push.
teaching_path.output: successive equal-time snapshots -> equal forward position advances; velocity unchanged.

teaching_path.action: Compare the released moving cart with a cart that starts at rest under the same zero-net-force condition.
teaching_path.why_valid: If both keep their initial velocities, the rule is about unchanged velocity rather than about rest.
teaching_path.output: moving cart: stays steady.  resting cart: stays at rest.  both show no velocity change.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A force must keep acting in the direction of motion or the object must stop.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A low-friction cart is pushed and then released. After the hand loses contact, what horizontal force is required merely to keep it moving steadily?
misconceptions.repair: Separate velocity from change of velocity: a net force is required for acceleration, not for the existence of motion.

exit_task.prompt: One cart is at rest and another moves steadily in a straight line. For each, decide whether zero net force is compatible with the motion and explain the common rule.

answer.summary: Zero net force is compatible with both. Each cart can keep its current velocity unchanged.
reasoning: Rest is a zero velocity that stays zero.
Steady straight motion is a nonzero velocity that stays unchanged.
The shared condition is no change of velocity, not no motion.
answer.check: Ask whether the motion description contains speeding up, slowing down, or turning. If none occurs, zero net force remains compatible.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The answer classifies motion qualitatively and asserts no computed force or acceleration.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created first-law contrast. It states no force equation and promotes no candidate-packet formula.

predict.prompt: A car cruises at a steady speed along a straight, level road with its engine running. Must the forward driving force be larger than the backward resistance just to keep it moving?
predict.defensible_answer: No. At steady velocity the net force is zero, so the forward and backward forces are equal in size.

attempt.produces: The total resistive force on the car with its direction, the net force on the car, and the car's velocity 10 s later, each justified from the steady 25 m/s.

rubric.criterion: Reads 'a steady 25 m/s in a straight line' as zero acceleration, so the net force is zero.
rubric.evidence_of: Separating motion from change of motion.

rubric.criterion: Finds the resistive total, 2000 N backward, from that balance rather than from the size of the speed.
rubric.evidence_of: Using the net-force condition to find an unknown force.

rubric.criterion: Keeps the velocity at 25 m/s in the same direction after 10 s.
rubric.evidence_of: Recognizing unchanged velocity, not rest, as what zero net force preserves.

accepted: The velocity is not changing, so the net force is zero and the resistive forces total 2000 N backward. With nothing changed, the car is still moving at 25 m/s in the same direction 10 s later.
rejected: 'The driving force must be bigger than the resistance, or the car would slow down.' At steady speed the net force is zero, so the two forces are equal.
'With zero net force the car is at rest 10 s later.' Zero net force keeps the velocity unchanged; it does not stop the car.

task.prompt: A 1500 kg car cruises at a steady 25 m/s along a straight, level road. The road pushes it forward with a driving force of 2000 N. Find the total resistive force and the net force on the car, and say what its velocity will be 10 s later if nothing changes.
givens: Mass 1500 kg; speed a steady 25 m/s in a straight line.
Resistive forces (air and rolling) act backward.

route.ask: What does 'a steady 25 m/s in a straight line' tell you about the car's acceleration?
route.why_this_ask: It separates 'is moving' from 'is changing its motion' before any force is discussed.

route.ask: So what must the net force on the car be?
route.why_this_ask: The net-force value is derived from the unchanged velocity, not assumed from the speed.

route.ask: The road pushes forward with 2000 N. What total backward force makes the net force zero?
route.why_this_ask: It finds the unknown resistance from the balance.

route.ask: If nothing changes for 10 s, can the velocity change? What is it then?
route.why_this_ask: It identifies unchanged velocity, not rest, as what zero net force keeps.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path compares a released moving cart with a resting cart. The learner route starts from the car's steady speed, derives the zero net force from it, and uses that to find the unknown resistance and the later velocity.

boundary_test.prompt: The driver eases off and the driving force drops to 500 N while the resistance is still 2000 N. Is the net force still zero, and what happens to the speed?
boundary_test.answer: No. The net force is 2000 − 500 = 1500 N backward, so the car slows at 1500/1500 = 1 m/s². Zero net force described only the steady interval.
boundary_test.confirms: Zero net force goes with unchanged velocity, not with motion as such.

construction_units.decision: Separate 'is moving' from 'is changing its velocity', and link zero net force only to the second.

independent_checks.statement: Put back a small friction force: the object must now slow down, which shows that a force changes the velocity rather than maintaining it.
a = F_net/m gives 0 N / m = 0 m/s², and distance equals speed × time in metres for equal time intervals.

compact_anchor.prompt: A 3 kg cart glides at 2 m/s on a frictionless track with no horizontal force on it. What is its velocity 5 s later?
compact_anchor.result: F_net = 0, so a = 0/3 = 0 and the velocity is still 2 m/s: zero net force keeps the motion unchanged, it does not stop it.

microtopics.title: Net force, not any one force, sets acceleration
microtopics.badge_reason: The difficult step is completing a one-body force inventory before using the simple equation.
entry_assumptions: Can choose one body, draw its external forces, and distinguish zero from nonzero net force.
microtopics.inferential_jump: For a chosen body of positive mass in the Grade 9 inertial-frame model, acceleration points with the signed net external force and satisfies F_net = m a.

teaching_path.action: Choose one body, declare a positive direction, and list only external forces acting on that body.
teaching_path.why_valid: The net-force relation applies to one body's external force sum.
teaching_path.output: one body; one signed axis; signed external-force list.

teaching_path.action: Add the signed forces to obtain F_net, then use F_net = m a.
teaching_path.why_valid: The net external force on the chosen body sets its acceleration: F_net = m a holds for that one body, with m > 0, in an inertial frame.
teaching_path.output: F_net = signed sum; a = F_net / m.

teaching_path.action: Return to an equal-opposite force case.
teaching_path.why_valid: The relation must recover zero acceleration when the signed force sum is zero.

teaching_path.action: Choose axes that make the active constraint easy to express; for a fixed inclined contact, use parallel/perpendicular axes when helpful, resolve the physical forces into those axes, and write separate signed Newton-II equations.
teaching_path.why_valid: Newton II is coordinate-independent. Aligning one axis with the contact makes maintained contact explicit as a_perp=0 while leaving the tangential acceleration free to be nonzero.
teaching_path.output: contact-aligned model: Sigma F_parallel = m a_parallel; Sigma F_perp = m a_perp, with maintained fixed contact -> a_perp = 0

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Acceleration points with whichever individual force looks largest in the diagram.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Two 10 N forces act opposite each other on a body. Does either force make the body accelerate in its direction?
misconceptions.repair: Add all signed external forces first; acceleration follows the net force, not an isolated arrow.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: If a block on a fixed incline has zero acceleration perpendicular to the plane, its total acceleration must be zero.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Can a block remain in contact with a fixed plane while speeding up down the plane?
misconceptions.repair: Yes. Maintained contact sets only a_perp=0. The parallel component a_parallel is determined independently by the net force along the plane.

exit_task.prompt: A 4 kg body has a net external force of +12 N along a declared axis. Find its acceleration.

reasoning: Use F_net = m a for the chosen body.
The positive sign matches the net-force direction.
answer.check: Multiplying 4 kg by +3 m/s^2 recovers +12 N.

microtopics.research_contribution: Author-created Grade 9 net-force calculation bound to the Newton-second-law gate and validator.

predict.prompt: A body moves right while its net external force points left. Which way is its acceleration?
predict.defensible_answer: Left, with the net force; velocity direction does not set acceleration direction.

attempt.produces: The signed net force on the car, its signed acceleration, and the time the car takes to stop.

rubric.criterion: Adds the friction and the drag with their signs before using F = ma.
rubric.evidence_of: Using the net external force rather than a selected force.

rubric.criterion: Keeps the acceleration negative (backward) while the velocity is positive.
rubric.evidence_of: Keeping direction through the component equation.

rubric.criterion: Uses the signed acceleration to find the stopping time, 20/5 = 4 s.
rubric.evidence_of: Linking the second law to the change in velocity.

accepted: F_net = −5400 − 600 = −6000 N, so a = −6000/1200 = −5 m/s². It stops after 20/5 = 4 s. The acceleration points backward while the velocity points forward.
rejected: 'The car moves forward, so its acceleration is +5 m/s².' The sign of the acceleration comes from the net force, not from the velocity.

task.prompt: A 1200 kg car moving at 20 m/s brakes. The road's friction on it is 5400 N backward and air drag is 600 N backward. Take forward as positive. Find the net force and the acceleration, and how long the car takes to stop if these forces stay constant.
givens: Road friction 5400 N backward; air drag 600 N backward.

route.ask: Which body is the equation about, and which horizontal forces act on it?
With forward positive, what is the signed sum of the road friction and the drag?
route.why_this_ask: It constructs the quantity the law uses: −6000 N.

route.ask: What acceleration does that net force give for the 1200 kg car, with its sign?
route.why_this_ask: It keeps the car's own mass and the sign together.

route.ask: The velocity is +20 m/s and the acceleration is negative. How long until the velocity reaches zero?
route.why_this_ask: It uses the signed acceleration to answer the stopping question.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The teaching path builds the force sum and returns to an equal-opposite case. The learner route builds a signed sum for a braking car and carries the signed acceleration to the stopping time.

boundary_test.prompt: Suppose the forces forward on the car add up to exactly 6000 N while the same 6000 N acts backward. What acceleration does F_net = ma give?
boundary_test.answer: Zero. The net force is zero, so the car keeps whatever velocity it has.
boundary_test.confirms: The second-law relation agrees with the first-law constant-velocity case.

construction_units.decision: Choose one body and a signed axis, add every external force on that body, and divide the net force by the mass; on a fixed incline, choose axes along and across the contact.

independent_checks.statement: The net force in newtons divided by the mass in kilograms must give m/s².
Flatten the incline to 0°: the method must give N = mg and no down-slope weight component, the level-floor case.

compact_anchor.prompt: A 5 kg trolley has 20 N forward and 5 N backward acting on it. What is its acceleration?
compact_anchor.result: F_net = 20 − 5 = 15 N forward, so a = 15/5 = 3 m/s² forward, in the direction of the net force.

microtopics.title: Quantitative static and kinetic friction conditions
microtopics.badge_reason: The difficult decision is not substituting mu N; it is determining the required tangential force, the actual normal reaction, and whether the contact can remain static.
entry_assumptions: Can determine friction direction from relative slip tendency.
Can write Newton-II equations for a chosen body.
microtopics.inferential_jump: Static friction is a responsive contact force: solve for the friction required to prevent relative slip and compare it with the limiting value mu_s N. Equality is a threshold condition, while the kinetic model is used only after sliding is established.

teaching_path.action: Build the chosen-body FBD and determine the normal reaction N from the force balance or acceleration perpendicular to the contact; do not assume N = mg.
teaching_path.why_valid: The normal reaction is the contact force needed by the actual perpendicular dynamics and can differ from mg when the surface is inclined or other forces have perpendicular components.

teaching_path.action: Assume no relative sliding provisionally and solve the tangential Newton-II equation for the static friction value f_required that would make that motion possible.
teaching_path.why_valid: Static friction takes the value required by the no-slip state, provided the contact can supply it.
The static-contact model permits any required value only up to the limiting magnitude.
teaching_path.output: |f_required| <= mu_s N -> static state feasible; |f_required| > mu_s N -> static state impossible

teaching_path.action: Use |f_s| = mu_s N only at impending slip; if relative sliding is already established, use |f_k| = mu_k N with direction opposing the relative sliding.
teaching_path.why_valid: The limiting equality and the sliding model describe different contact states and are not unconditional identities.
teaching_path.output: impending slip -> |f_s| = mu_s N; sliding -> |f_k| = mu_k N

misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A small horizontal force is applied to a block that remains at rest. Must static friction already equal mu_s N?
misconceptions.repair: No. First solve the force required for no slip. Static friction matches that requirement up to its limit; equality occurs only at impending slip.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The normal force is always mg.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: If an extra force presses a block into a horizontal surface, can the normal reaction still be assumed equal to mg?
misconceptions.repair: Determine N from the perpendicular free-body equation. N = mg is only a special case.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: If both mu_s and mu_k are given, the coefficients themselves tell you which friction model to use.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: A problem gives both mu_s and mu_k but does not say whether the contact slips. Can you choose kinetic friction just because mu_k is supplied?
misconceptions.repair: No. Determine the contact state first: test whether the no-slip friction demand fits within mu_s N. Use the kinetic model only after sliding is established.

exit_task.prompt: A contact has known normal reaction N and coefficient mu_s. The no-slip force equation requires tangential friction f_required. State the test for whether static contact is possible, when equality with mu_s N is justified, and what changes once sliding is established.

answer.summary: Static contact is possible when |f_required| <= mu_s N. Equality |f_s| = mu_s N is justified only at impending slip. After relative sliding is established, use the kinetic model |f_k| = mu_k N with direction opposite the relative sliding.
reasoning: Static friction supplies the required no-slip value rather than an automatic maximum.
The limiting value mu_s N is a bound and becomes an equality only at the threshold of slipping.
The kinetic model belongs to a different contact state: established relative sliding.
answer.check: If f_required = 0, the rule must allow f_s = 0 even when mu_s N is nonzero; that falsifies the unconditional f = mu N shortcut.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit compares a symbolic friction demand with a symbolic static bound and distinguishes contact states; no numerical force is computed.

microtopics.research_contribution: ExamSIDE friction-threshold demand justifies a separate quantitative contact-state decision while preserving the qualitative friction-direction capability as its prerequisite.

predict.prompt: A block remains at rest while the applied tangential force is gradually increased. Before impending slip, must static friction already equal mu_s N?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Static friction adjusts to the value required to prevent relative slip, up to the limit mu_s N.

attempt.produces: For each trial: the normal force, the static limit, a decision whether the box moves, the friction and the acceleration.
attempt.model_response: Find N from the FBD, solve for f_required under no slip, compare |f_required| with mu_s N, and use the kinetic model only after sliding is established.

task.prompt: A 5 kg box rests on a floor with μ_s = 0.5 and μ_k = 0.4; take g = 10 m/s². A 30 N horizontal push is applied. Decide whether the box moves, and find the friction and the acceleration. Then repeat with a second child pressing straight down on the lid with 20 N while the same 30 N push acts.
givens: Mass 5 kg; μ_s = 0.5; μ_k = 0.4; g = 10 m/s².
Second trial: an extra 20 N downward press.

accepted: Trial 1: N = 50 N, limit 25 N < 30 N, so the box slides; friction is 0.4 × 50 = 20 N and a = (30 − 20)/5 = 2 m/s². Trial 2: N = 70 N, limit 35 N ≥ 30 N, so the box stays at rest with 30 N of static friction.

route.ask: In each trial, what normal force does the vertical balance give?
route.why_this_ask: The limit depends on the real N (50 N, then 70 N), not on mg alone.

route.ask: If the box did not slip, what friction would the 30 N push require?
route.why_this_ask: Static friction is set by the need of the no-slip state before the limit is tested.

route.ask: Is 30 N within μ_s N in each trial?
route.why_this_ask: The inequality decides whether the no-slip state is possible (25 N, then 35 N).

route.ask: In the trial where the box slides, which friction model applies, and what acceleration results?
route.why_this_ask: It separates established sliding (μ_k N) from static friction.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The learner begins by testing an assumed no-slip state and lets the inequality accept or reject it; the completed teaching path states the contact-state rules explicitly.

boundary_test.prompt: If the no-slip equation requires zero friction while mu_s N is positive, what is the static-friction magnitude?
boundary_test.answer: Zero. Static friction need not sit at its maximum.
boundary_test.confirms: The static relation is an inequality/response rule, not an unconditional equality.

construction_units.decision: Find the actual normal force and the friction that rest would need, compare that need with μ_s N, and use μ N as the friction value only at impending slip or once sliding.

independent_checks.statement: Put the friction and acceleration back into the horizontal equation: the pull minus the friction must equal mass times acceleration in each case.
Set the pull to zero: the method must return zero friction, not μ_s N, and zero acceleration.

compact_anchor.prompt: A 2 kg block on a floor with μ_s = 0.5 and μ_k = 0.3 is pulled horizontally with 14 N (g = 10 m/s²). Does it stay put, and what is its acceleration?
compact_anchor.result: N = 20 N, so static friction can give at most 10 N; 14 N > 10 N, so it slides. Then f_k = 0.3 × 20 = 6 N and a = (14 − 6)/2 = 4 m/s².

relations.meaning: The vector net external force on a chosen body equals its mass times its acceleration.

symbols.meaning: Net external force along the declared axis
Mass of the chosen body
Acceleration along the same axis

conditions: F_net and a refer to the same chosen body.
All signed components use one declared axis.

derivation.action: Choose one body, declare a positive direction, and add the signed external forces acting on that body.
derivation.why_valid: Newton's second law uses the net external force on one chosen body.
derivation.output: F_net = signed sum of external forces on the chosen body.

derivation.action: Set the signed net force equal to mass times signed acceleration.
derivation.why_valid: Newton's second law equates the net force on one body with its mass times its acceleration, in an inertial frame.

limits: Do not mix forces acting on different bodies in one force sum.
The simple Grade 9 use assumes an inertial frame and constant positive mass.
checks: Equal opposite forces give F_net = 0 and therefore a = 0.
For fixed mass, reversing F_net reverses a.

relations.meaning: For a contact that remains static, the static-friction magnitude adjusts to the value required by the tangential dynamics up to the limiting value mu_s N; equality applies only at impending slip.

symbols.meaning: Signed static friction force along the contact tangent
Coefficient of static friction for the contact model
Normal contact-force magnitude obtained from the actual perpendicular dynamics

conditions: The surfaces are in contact and have no relative sliding during the state being tested.
N is obtained from the actual free-body dynamics, not assumed to equal mg.
Static friction opposes the impending relative slip direction.
Equality |f_s| = mu_s N is used only at impending slip.

derivation.action: Solve the no-slip tangential dynamics for the friction value required by that assumed state.
derivation.why_valid: Static friction is responsive to the tangential force demand.
derivation.output: f_s = f_required under the provisional no-slip state

derivation.action: Compare the required magnitude with mu_s N.
derivation.why_valid: The contact can sustain the static state only within its limiting friction magnitude.

limits: This is not an unconditional equality.
It does not determine N; N comes from the perpendicular force equation.
It does not apply after relative sliding is established.
checks: A zero tangential demand permits f_s = 0 even if mu_s N is positive.
At impending slip the inequality reaches equality.

relations.meaning: Once relative sliding at the contact is established, the bounded dry-sliding model uses kinetic-friction magnitude mu_k N, directed opposite the relative sliding.

symbols.meaning: Signed kinetic friction force along the contact tangent
Coefficient of kinetic friction for the declared contact model
Normal contact-force magnitude from the actual perpendicular dynamics

conditions: Relative sliding between the two surfaces is established.
N is obtained from the actual free-body dynamics.
The friction direction opposes the relative sliding at the contact.
The simple dry-sliding coefficient model is being used.

derivation.action: Confirm that the contact is sliding and determine N from the perpendicular dynamics.
derivation.why_valid: The kinetic model is state-specific and depends on the actual normal reaction.

derivation.action: Set the kinetic-friction magnitude to mu_k N and assign its sign opposite the relative sliding.
derivation.why_valid: That is the declared bounded kinetic-friction model.
derivation.output: |f_k| = mu_k N with direction opposite relative sliding

limits: Do not use this relation to decide whether static contact can persist.

Equal tension is what causes the equal-magnitude fixed-pulley acceleration constraint.

questions.stem: An ice-hockey puck of mass 0.2 kg slides across smooth ice at 4 m/s after the stick loses contact. Friction and air resistance are negligible. What horizontal forces act on it, what is its velocity 3 s later, and would a puck at rest on the same ice start moving?
conditions: Friction and air resistance are negligible.
The ice is horizontal.

answer.summary: No horizontal force acts. The puck still moves at 4 m/s, having covered 12 m, and a puck at rest stays at rest.
reasoning: Once the stick loses contact, nothing touches the puck horizontally, so the horizontal net force is zero.
F_net = m a gives a = 0/0.2 = 0 m/s², so the velocity does not change: after 3 s it is still 4 m/s.
Equal times give equal advances: 4 m in each second, 12 m in 3 s.
A puck at rest under the same zero net force keeps its zero velocity, so it stays at rest.
answer.check: With even a small friction force added, the puck would slow down: the force changes the velocity rather than keeping it up.

questions.stem: An 80 kg skydiver falls at a steady 50 m/s. Take g = 10 m/s². Find the air resistance on the skydiver and the net force. Just after the parachute opens, the skydiver is still moving downward but slowing: is the net force then zero, upward or downward?
conditions: The steady fall is in a straight vertical line.
g = 10 m/s².

answer.summary: In the steady fall the air resistance is 800 N upward and the net force is zero. Just after the parachute opens the net force points upward, even though the skydiver is still moving down.
reasoning: A steady 50 m/s means the velocity is not changing, so the net force is zero.
Weight = 80 × 10 = 800 N down, so the air resistance must be 800 N up.
After the parachute opens the downward velocity is shrinking, so the acceleration, and with it the net force, points upward.
answer.check: The size of the velocity plays no part: the same zero net force would hold at a steady 5 m/s or at rest. Only a change of velocity needs a net force.

hints.text: During the steady fall, is the skydiver's velocity changing?
Zero net force goes with an unchanging velocity, however large; a slowing fall is a change of velocity, so ask which way that change points.

hint_ladder.text: Draw the skydiver twice, in the steady fall and just after the parachute opens, each with a velocity arrow and a separate net-force arrow. Leave the net-force arrow empty where the velocity is not changing.

questions.failure_signal: You said the steady fall needs a net downward force because the skydiver is moving down, or that the net force stays downward after the parachute opens: the net force follows the change of velocity, not the velocity.

family_exposure.closure: Established: zero net force means an unchanging velocity, and a slowing motion has a net force opposite the velocity. Later tasks read steady straight motion as a balanced-force state.

difficulty.basis: Use steady fall to establish force balance, then reinterpret the net-force direction immediately after the parachute changes the motion.

questions.stem: A 10 kg crate rests on a rough horizontal floor with μ_s = 0.75; take g = 10 m/s². A rope on the crate can be pulled horizontally, at 37° above the horizontal, or at 53° above the horizontal (sin 37° = cos 53° = 0.6, cos 37° = sin 53° = 0.8). For each direction, find the smallest pull that starts the crate sliding. A worker can pull with at most 61 N: in which of the three directions can the worker start the crate?
conditions: The crate stays in contact with the floor in every direction.
Resolve each pull into horizontal and vertical components.
The pull is the unknown: do not take N = mg before the vertical balance is written.

answer.summary: When the crate is just about to slide, the friction it needs equals the limit μ_s N, and N = 100 − P sin θ. So P cos θ = 0.75(100 − P sin θ), which gives P = 75/(cos θ + 0.75 sin θ). Horizontal: 75 N. At 37°: 75/1.25 = 60 N. At 53°: 75/1.2 = 62.5 N. The 37° pull needs the least, and a worker limited to 61 N can start the crate only in that direction.
reasoning: With a pull P at angle θ above the horizontal, the vertical balance gives N = mg − P sin θ = 100 − P sin θ.
Until the crate moves, friction must equal the horizontal part P cos θ; the smallest starting pull makes that need equal to the limit: P cos θ = 0.75(100 − P sin θ).
Only the 37° threshold, 60 N, is within the worker's 61 N; horizontally 75 N is needed, and at 53° 62.5 N.
answer.check: At 37° with P = 60 N: horizontal part 48 N, vertical part 36 N, so N = 64 N and μ_s N = 48 N, exactly the need. At 53° with P = 61 N: need 61 × 0.6 = 36.6 N, but N = 100 − 48.8 = 51.2 N gives a limit of 38.4 N, so the crate stays at rest.

rubric.criterion: Writes N = 100 − P sin θ with the pull still unknown, before using the limit.
rubric.evidence_of: The static limit depends on the actual contact force, which here depends on the pull.

rubric.criterion: Sets the need P cos θ equal to μ_s N only at the start of sliding and finds 75 N, 60 N and 62.5 N.
rubric.evidence_of: Turning the no-slip test into a threshold for an unknown force.

rubric.criterion: Decides that only the 37° direction works for a 61 N worker.
rubric.evidence_of: Comparing thresholds across directions instead of assuming more tilt is always better or always worse.

reasoning_route.action: Write N from the vertical balance with the pull unknown: N = 100 − P sin θ.
reasoning_route.why_valid: The crate has no vertical acceleration, and the upward part of the pull carries part of the weight.
inputs: pull P at θ above the horizontal

reasoning_route.action: At the smallest starting pull the need equals the limit: P cos θ = 0.75(100 − P sin θ).
reasoning_route.why_valid: Below that pull static friction can supply the need; at it, the need reaches μ_s N.

reasoning_route.action: Evaluate the threshold in each direction (75 N, 60 N, 62.5 N) and compare with the worker's 61 N.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Tilting lowers N but also the horizontal part, so the threshold must be computed, not guessed, for each direction.
reasoning_route.output: Only the 37° pull can start the crate.

reasoning_route.action: Substitute P = 60 N at 37° into both force equations.
reasoning_route.why_valid: At the threshold, the vertical balance holds and the need equals μ_s N.

adaptation.reason: Change the earlier threshold exercise so that the pull is the unknown, lowers N as it grows, and must be compared across directions.

transfer.statement: The learner must turn the no-slip test into a threshold for an unknown pull that also changes N, and compare that threshold across directions, instead of deciding the state for a given pull.
transfer.invariant: N from the actual vertical balance and the comparison of the friction needed with μ_s N carry over; what changes is that the pull is unknown and its direction is the choice.

checked_against: Q-PHY-NLM-1A-FRICTION-TEST-01 (Core1A worked anchor): given horizontal pulls on a 4 kg box, N = mg; the state is decided for each given pull.
Q-PHY-NLM-1A-FRICTION-DIRECTION-01 (Core1A worked anchor): the book on the tray never slips; only the friction's direction and size are found.
MIC-PHY-NLM-FRICTION-QUANT Core1B attempt: a given 30 N push on a 5 kg box, then with a 20 N downward press; the state is decided for each given push, and N is changed by a separate force.
MIC-PHY-NLM-FRICTION-QUANT Core1B boundary test: a zero friction need against a positive limit.
MIC-PHY-NLM-FRICTION Core1B attempt: a block pressed on a wall; the press sets only the limit.
Q-PHY-NLM-2A-FRICTION-THRESHOLD-01 (Core2A): a no-slip threshold for stacked blocks with N = mg, so the force does not change N.
Q-PHY-NLM-2A-FRICTION-ZERO-08, -STATIC-09, -KINETIC-10 and Q-PHY-NLM-2A-COV-04 (Core2A): the state is given or no threshold is sought.
Q-PHY-NLM-INCLINE-2A-STATIC-02 and -SLIDING-03 (Core2A): an incline rest condition or stated sliding, with no applied pull.
Q-PHY-NLM-2B-FRICTION-ANGLED-THRESHOLD-04 (Core2B): a push below the horizontal, whose tilt only raises N and the threshold; there is no best direction.
novelty.why_new: Every earlier friction item either gives the pull and asks for the state, gives the state, or asks for one threshold whose tilt only makes things worse. Here the pull is unknown and lowers N as it grows, and its direction is the choice. Tilting upward first helps and then hurts: the smallest starting pull is 75 N, 60 N and 62.5 N at 0°, 37° and 53°. The learner must compute and compare a threshold for each direction and finds that the best one is neither horizontal nor the steepest.

hint_ladder.text: Draw the crate for one direction with its weight, N, the pull split into horizontal and vertical parts, and a friction arrow labelled f. Keep the pull as P, not a number.

questions.failure_signal: You found 75 N for every direction because you kept N = mg = 100 N: the upward part of the pull lightens the contact. Or you chose 53° because it lightens the contact most: its horizontal part shrinks faster, so it needs 62.5 N, more than the 60 N at 37°.

family_exposure.closure: Established: tilting a pull upward trades horizontal drive against a lighter contact, so the smallest pull that starts a body comes at an in-between angle, not horizontally or at the steepest angle.

difficulty.basis: The pull is an unknown threshold that also changes the normal reaction, and three directions must be compared before the feasible choice is made.

teaching_routes.title: Reveal Grade-9 Newton-law spine with bounded friction/connection preparation and frame extension
entry_needs: Can tell whether an object's velocity is changing; the specific turning-point diagnostic from Motion is not a prerequisite.
learner_actions: Separate motion from change of motion.
Keep individual forces distinct from their net result.
Assign each force to the body on which it acts.
Determine friction direction from relative slip tendency.
Use signed net external force with F_net = m a.
Test static friction against its limit before using a limiting or kinetic formula.
Apply a common acceleration only when an active connection keeps the relevant separation fixed.
Use one common tension magnitude only under explicit ideal-string/redirection assumptions.
Derive the one-fixed-pulley acceleration relation from constant string length rather than a pulley-count rule.
Keep Newton-third-law partner forces on different bodies.
Use observer-frame/pseudo-force reasoning only when an explicit extension question demands it.
help_plan: Use a released low-friction cart for the first-law contrast.
Use two separate body inventories before any force equations.
For friction, ask for N and f_required before revealing any coefficient formula.
For connected bodies, ask what physical condition keeps the relative separation fixed.
For a string/pulley task, require the ideal assumptions and actual length equation before any tension or acceleration shortcut.
Use roadside versus accelerating-bus descriptions for the observer boundary.
teaching_routes.reveal_plan: Completed constructions are visible only after body ownership, contact state, connection model and any string geometry are declared; coefficient and constraint relations are never presented as unconditional apparatus formulas.

source_preferences.reason: The four rungs are authored here without promoting candidate-packet authority.

when_not_suitable: Do not treat accelerating-frame/pseudo-force reasoning as ordinary Grade-9 Standard syllabus content.
Do not infer momentum-conservation or collision content from the presence of Newton's laws.
Do not use the single-fixed-pulley relation for movable/compound pulley geometry.
Do not assume equal tension after an ideal-string or ideal-redirection assumption is broken.

teaching_routes.title: Elicit Grade-9 Newton-law spine with bounded friction/connection preparation and frame extension
entry_needs: Same intrinsic Grade-9 force-law coverage as Core1A; no inferred learner mastery and no turning-point prerequisite.
learner_actions: Predict whether zero net force can coexist with steady motion.
Build body-specific force inventories before combining forces.
Predict friction direction from contact slip tendency.
Use the net force to predict acceleration.
Decide whether a static contact can supply the required friction before selecting a coefficient equality.
Name the connection that justifies a common acceleration.
Earn one tension symbol by stating the ideal-string model.
Reconstruct the one-fixed-pulley acceleration relation from constant string length.
Separate Newton-third-law partners by body.
Enter observer-frame reconstruction only for explicit extension demand.
help_plan: Ask which body receives each force before naming any pairing rule.
Ask what friction value the no-slip equations require before asking about a coefficient limit.
Ask which relative separation is fixed before offering a common acceleration.
Ask which string segments actually change length before offering a pulley relation.
Ask whether a physical agent changed before introducing a pseudo-force.
teaching_routes.reveal_plan: Prediction, reconstruction, misconception diagnosis and boundary tests precede the closed reveal.

source_preferences.reason: Each elicitation cycle is authored specifically for the corresponding rung.

when_not_suitable: Do not substitute a declarative diagram for the learner's body-ownership decision.
Do not present pseudo-force/frame-choice content as ordinary Grade-9 Standard syllabus material.
Do not hand over mu N as the friction value before the learner decides the contact state.
Do not hand over equal tension or an acceleration ratio without the model/geometry that justifies it.

application_contexts.title: Block on a fixed inclined plane
application_contexts.description: A rigid plane at angle theta to the horizontal used as an application context for body-specific FBDs, contact-aligned axes, force decomposition, Newton II, normal reaction and friction-state reasoning.
invariants: The plane is fixed unless a question explicitly states otherwise.
One may choose axes parallel and perpendicular to the plane without changing the physical forces.
For maintained contact with a fixed plane, the body's acceleration perpendicular to the plane is zero.
The normal reaction is determined by the perpendicular dynamics; it is not automatically mg.
If friction is present, its direction and model are determined from relative sliding or slip tendency at the contact.

variation_dimensions.name: plane_angle
variation_dimensions.description: Vary theta while keeping the same fixed-plane geometry.

variation_dimensions.name: surface_state
variation_dimensions.description: Vary smooth, static-rough, impending-slip and established-sliding contact.

variation_dimensions.name: applied_force_direction
variation_dimensions.description: Vary forces parallel to the plane, horizontal, or otherwise angled so the normal reaction may change.

variation_dimensions.name: representation
variation_dimensions.description: Vary contact-aligned versus laboratory horizontal/vertical axes while preserving the same physical situation.

task_objectives: Build a correct chosen-body force account without inventing component forces as extra interactions.
Resolve the required force components relative to the declared axes.
Use perpendicular dynamics to determine N and tangential dynamics to determine acceleration or required friction.
Check friction feasibility or sliding state only after the contact-normal dynamics are established.
scope_limits: No moving wedge or accelerating-plane constraint.
